deep.reconstruction:
There is no mathematics on this page: no formulas, computations or derivations. It is a sheet of philosophical reading notes, mostly excerpts and paraphrases, taken by Riemann from J. F. Herbart's Allgemeine Metaphysik. The context points there: the previous page cites 'W. III, 492' and 'Met. Schlussanmerkung zum ersten Theil', and this page carries the marginal page numbers S.494 and S.496. The content runs as follows.

(1) Plato's 'matter' (the receptacle of the Timaeus) is pure possibility, 'das Könnende', presupposed before the actual existence of a thing. Plato then thinks this possibility as something spatial, so it becomes extended stuff, Materie.

(2) Leibniz and Plato are contrasted. The Leibniz-Wolff school seeks the real in matter and finds it in monads. Plato places the real outside matter, but is forced to grant changing things a semblance of reality. Herbart's diagnosis is that Plato saw the contradiction in the concept of change. Leibniz only wanted to avoid the causa transiens and never saw change itself as the problem.

(3) The historical link between the two runs through Aristotle's composition of the sensible thing from matter and form. Riemann gives a German rendering of Metaphysics VII(Z).3, 1029a: substance is that which is not predicated of something else. Matter, stripped of all determinations, would seem to be substance, but it cannot be. Form (eidos) and the compound therefore have a better claim. Riemann adds the remark that Aristotle always presupposes the reality of sensible things.

(4) Later the motive of the Ideas, the contradiction of change, was forgotten. The habit of splitting things into 'what' (essence) and 'being' (existence) remained, along with the scholastic principle 'essentiae rerum sunt aeternae et immutabiles'. Existence then became a mere modus, the complementum possibilitatis. The concept of the possible, which Plato had assigned to matter, migrated onto essence.

(5) A note on Aristotle's report about Protagoras, Democritus, Empedocles and Anaxagoras. Riemann cites it as 'Cap. V lib III'; in modern numbering it is Met. IV(Γ).5, 1009b. Their sensualism leads to the conclusion that seeking truth is like 'chasing flying birds'. Herbart's diagnosis is that they took the sensible alone for being.

(6) Aristotle Met. I(A).6 on the three sources of Plato's doctrine: Pythagoreanism, opposition to Heraclitus via Cratylus, and Socratic definition. Riemann quotes 987b6, that there can be no common definition of sensibles since they are always changing. He also paraphrases 987b27-29: Plato set numbers apart from sensibles, whereas the Pythagoreans said numbers are the things themselves. The sentence continues onto the next page with the condition under which Plato could admit numbers as real.

The page belongs to Riemann's study of Herbart's metaphysics and the theory of space and matter, which forms the background of his natural-philosophical fragments. It contains no mathematical problem.
errors: No mathematical errors, since there is no mathematics on the page.

The citation 'Cap. V lib III Metaphysicorum' corresponds to Met. IV (Γ).5, 1009b in modern Bekker numbering. Some older editions numbered the books differently, so this is an edition convention rather than a slip by Riemann.
The Greek quotation from Met. I.6, 987b6, is reproduced essentially correctly. The 'Metaphysicorum VII,3' citation for the paraphrase of 1029a is correct.

results.what: Excerpts and paraphrases of Herbart's historical critique (Allgemeine Metaphysik, Schlussanmerkung) of Plato's matter, Aristotle's matter/form, the scholastic essentia/existentia distinction, and Leibniz's monads.
results.modern_name: History of philosophy and metaphysics (not mathematics)
results.usually_credited_to: J. F. Herbart (Allgemeine Metaphysik, 1828-29), citing Aristotle Met. I.6, IV.5, VII.3

deep.surprise_reason: These are reading notes copied or paraphrased from Herbart's Metaphysik. Riemann's study of Herbart is well documented in the published Naturphilosophie fragments and by scholars such as Scholz. There is no mathematical content.
transcription_corrections: A marginal page reference 'S.496' stands at the right edge beside the paragraph beginning 'Da nun späterhin'. The transcription omits it.

The line 'Aristoteles: Heraklit = (Kratyl[?]): Euklid[?]' is doubtful. The final word is unclear in the image and more likely refers to Sokrates or a page reference (a 'Fest./Fol.'-type abbreviation) than to Euklid. The opening struck words '[-Zu Seite-]' are uncertain.
'Im Ganzen ist ihre positiven Lehrsatzungen' should probably read 'Im Ganzen ihrer positiven Lehrsätze (Lehrsatzungen)'.

'konnte jenes Können eigentlich nur gegen, was unter dem complementum possibilitatis...' is garbled. The sense in Herbart is roughly 'konnte jenes Können eigentlich nur fragen lassen, was unter dem complementum possibilitatis solle verstanden werden'.
The superscript εἶδος is written above 'und', glossing 'Qualität'. The text reads 'die Qualität (εἶδος) und das aus beiden'.
